summary: Glucose data over 14 days shows good CGM coverage but no carbohydrate entries. The main issues are overnight hypoglycemia (up to 18.5% time below 70 mg/dL around 01:00 local time) and afternoon hyperglycemia (up to 32.1% time above 180 mg/dL around 16:00). The loop frequently reduces or zeros basal at night, suggesting the 00:00–05:00 basal rate of 0.6 U/h is too high. Daytime highs cannot be attributed to basal or CR without meal data. Several AAPS safety limits are set far above clinical needs, posing a latent overdose risk.

analysis_steps.findings: The 00:00–05:00 basal rate of 0.6 U/h is likely too high; the loop frequently sets zero basal during this period, yet overnight hypoglycemia persists. After 05:00, glucose stabilizes. Daytime rises after 08:00 may be meal-driven, not basal-related. The overnight target of 90 mg/dL may be low but basal reduction is the priority.

DIA 10 h is typical for rapid-acting analogs and shows no evidence of stacking. Correction boluses often produce large drops, confirming high insulin sensitivity.

The loop frequently suspends basal overnight, confirming that the profile basal is too high. SMB doses are very small (0.05 U) and do not cause stacking. Safety limits (max basal 12 U/h, max IOB 25 U) are disproportionately large relative to actual needs, presenting a latent overdose risk.

recommendations.title: Reduce overnight basal rate
recommendations.description: The 00:00-05:00 basal rate of 0.6 U/h causes recurring nocturnal hypoglycemia. The loop often zeroes basal during this window, indicating excess insulin. Reducing this rate should lower hypoglycemia risk without worsening daytime control.

recommendations.title: Tighten max basal and max IOB safety limits
recommendations.description: The current max basal (12 U/h) and max IOB (25 U) far exceed clinically plausible values for someone with TDI ~20 U. In the event of a software or hardware failure, these limits could permit a massive insulin overdose. Reducing them to 3 U/h and 5 U respectively adds a critical safety layer without impairing daily control.

recommendations.title: Begin carbohydrate logging
recommendations.description: Without any carbohydrate entries, CR, meal timing, and post-prandial optimization cannot be performed. Logging all meals for at least 7-14 days is necessary before any meal-related adjustments can be considered.

profile_recommendation.recommendation: Reduce profile basal 00:00-05:00 from 0.6 U/h to 0.5 U/h.
profile_recommendation.rationale: Hourly glucose local data show 18.5% TBR at 01:00 with frequent zero basal commands from the loop, indicating basal excess. This change directly addresses the primary safety issue without affecting later time blocks.
profile_recommendation.next_check: After applying the change, monitor overnight CGM for 3 consecutive nights. If TBR persists above 5%, consider a further reduction to 0.45 U/h or raising the overnight target to 100 mg/dL.

parameter_decisions.rationale: Current limits vastly exceed any safe requirement (typical basal 0.6–0.8 U/h, total daily insulin ~20 U). In a malfunction, 12 U/h could cause fatal hypoglycemia. Reducing to 3 U/h and 5 U provides essential safety while still far exceeding normal needs.

implementation_steps: 1. Discuss the proposed overnight basal reduction (0.6 U/h to 0.5 U/h for 00:00-05:00) with your care team.

2. Once agreed, apply the basal change and monitor overnight CGM for 3 nights. If time below 70 mg/dL remains above 5%, consider a further small reduction or raising the overnight target to 100 mg/dL.
3. After overnight glucose has stabilized, update the AAPS safety limits: set max basal to 3 U/h and max IOB to 5 U. This reduces latent overdose risk without affecting daily control.
4. Begin entering all carbohydrate amounts and meal times into AAPS. Continue for at least 2 weeks before revisiting CR, ISF, and meal timing optimization.
5. After sufficient meal data, re-run TuneMyBG to evaluate CR segments, prebolus timing, and whether e-carbs could help with any absorption delays.
education: Overnight hypoglycemia can be caused by basal insulin that is too high relative to the body's needs; reducing basal rate is often more effective than raising the target.

Safety limits (max basal and max IOB) are fail-safes that prevent the pump from delivering dangerously high insulin doses if the algorithm or hardware malfunctions. They should be set just above the highest daily need, not to 12 U/h and 25 U.
Carbohydrate logging is essential for automated insulin delivery systems to calculate meal boluses and adjust CR/ISF. Without it, the system cannot learn post-prandial patterns.
safety_notes: This is decision-support content only. All suggested changes must be reviewed with your healthcare provider before implementation.
Make only one change at a time and monitor glucose closely for at least 2-3 days to assess its effect before making another adjustment.
If you experience severe hypoglycemia (requiring assistance) or persistent unexplained lows, contact your care team immediately.
